lessons.title: Components, velocity and flight events
lessons.summary: Use one clock and two component equations, then check that the event happens in flight.
lessons.objective: Resolve a projectile into horizontal and vertical motion and find physically valid event times.
lessons.before: Review constant-acceleration equations, resolving a velocity and solving quadratic equations. Distinguish displacement, velocity and speed. All angles in a calculation must use one consistent angular unit.
lessons.ideas:
State the model and the axes

During free flight, model the object as a particle with no air resistance and constant gravitational acceleration. Take rightwards and upwards as positive. Write \(g\gt 0\) for the magnitude of gravity. Numerical exercises here explicitly use \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

If the initial components are \(a,b\) and the initial position is \((x_0,y_0)\), constant acceleration gives

\[\begin{gathered}x=x_0+at,\qquad y=y_0+bt-\frac12gt^2\\v_x=a,\qquad v_y=b-gt\\v=\sqrt{a^2+(b-gt)^2}\end{gathered}\]

For speed \(u\) and an angle \(\theta\) above the rightward horizontal, \(a=u\cos\theta\) and \(b=u\sin\theta\). A downward launch has a negative upward component. Acceleration remains downward after the highest point.

The highest point is a vertical event

Set \(v_y=0\), not the whole speed equal to zero. For \(b\gt 0\),

\[\begin{gathered}t_{\rm top}=\frac bg,\qquad y_{\rm top}=y_0+\frac{b^2}{2g}\end{gathered}\]

The minimum speed is \(|a|\) if the highest point belongs to the flight being considered. Returning to the launch height gives the nonzero time \(2b/g\). That formula does not give the landing time on ground below a raised platform: solve the actual ground-height equation.

Direction and perpendicular directions

When \(a\gt 0\), the signed direction gradient is \((b-gt)/a\). State whether the direction is above or below the horizontal. For a leftward velocity, the gradient alone does not specify the quadrant. For two non-vertical directions, perpendicularity means that the gradients multiply to \(-1\); after clearing the denominators the condition is

\[\begin{gathered}a^2+(b-gt_1)(b-gt_2)=0\end{gathered}\]

Check vertical cases separately if a denominator is zero. The displayed component identity also handles a perpendicularity condition without dividing by a velocity.

Algebraic roots need a physical interval

A height can be crossed twice, on the way up and down. Keep every positive root that occurs before the first ground impact. A speed inferred from an observation is invalid if the object would already have landed. For a concave height quadratic, positive height at both ends of an interval ensures positive height throughout it.
lessons.method:
1. Choose axes, initial height and a time origin.
  2. Resolve the initial velocity and write both position and velocity components.
  3. Translate the event into an equation: height, vertical velocity, speed or direction.
  4. Solve for every candidate and check the first-impact interval.
  5. Give exact components or speed, direction and SI units as requested.
mistakes: Gravity changes vertical velocity, not the horizontal component in this model.
At the apex the vertical component is zero; the speed need not be zero.
The usual double-ascent flight time applies only to a return to the launch height.
A negative vertical component indicates downward motion, not a negative speed.
An algebraic root describing an observation after landing is inadmissible.

examples.title: 1 · Position, velocity and speed are different answers
examples.question: A particle starts at ground level with velocity components \(9\) rightwards and \(12\) upwards, in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find its position and velocity after one second, and its speed.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}x=9t,\qquad y=12t-5t^2\\t=1:\quad(x,y)=(9,7)\\(v_x,v_y)=(9,2),\qquad v=\sqrt{85}\end{gathered}\]

Distances are in metres and velocity components in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The particle is still rising because its vertical component is positive. Its first return to ground is at \(t=\frac{12}{5}\) s.

examples.title: 2 · Landing below the launch level
examples.question: A particle is launched from a platform \(24\) m above ground. Its components are \(8\) rightwards and \(7\) upwards, in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). With \(g=10\), find its landing time, horizontal travel and impact velocity.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}0=24+7t-5t^2\\(5t+8)(t-3)=0\\t=3,\quad x=24,\quad v_y=7-30=-23\\v_x=8,\qquad v=\sqrt{593}\end{gathered}\]

The negative root is outside this flight. The impact velocity points right and down; the speed is positive. Doubling the ascent time would return to the platform height, not ground level.

examples.title: 3 · Two crossings and the least speed
examples.question: A particle has initial components \(20\) rightwards and \(15\) upwards, from ground level. Take \(g=10\). Find when it is \(10\) m high, the separation of those positions, and its least speed.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}10=15t-5t^2\\(t-1)(t-2)=0,\qquad t=1,2\\\Delta x=20(2-1)=20\\t_{\rm top}=\frac32,\qquad v_{\min}=20\end{gathered}\]

The flight ends at \(t=3\), so both crossings are valid. The vertical components at them are \(5\) and \(-5\); their directions are equally inclined above and below the horizontal.

examples.title: 4 · Infer components, then check the observations
examples.question: A particle starts \(20\) m above ground, moving rightwards. Its speeds at \(t=1\) s and \(t=3\) s are \(\sqrt{65}\) and \(\sqrt{305}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Take \(g=10\). Find its initial components and check that both observations can occur before landing.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}a^2+(b-10)^2=65\\a^2+(b-30)^2=305\\800-40b=240,\qquad b=14\\a^2=49,\quad a=7\\y(3)=20+42-45=17\end{gathered}\]

Choose \(a=7\) because the motion is rightwards. The first landing time is \(\frac{7+\sqrt{149}}5\gt 3\) s. The positive initial and final heights, together with concavity, confirm that no earlier ground contact invalidates these observations.

lessons.title: Cartesian trajectories, targets and obstacles
lessons.summary: Eliminate time, retain every launch angle and apply the precise contact rule.
lessons.objective: Use a trajectory equation to find launch settings and complete physically valid obstacle intervals.
lessons.before: Complete components and flight events. Review quadratic inequalities and the discriminant.
lessons.ideas:
Eliminate the same time from both components

If \(a\ne0\), use \(t=(x-x_0)/a\) in the vertical equation:

\[\begin{gathered}y=y_0+\frac ba(x-x_0)-\frac g{2a^2}(x-x_0)^2\end{gathered}\]

For a rightward launch at an acute angle, set \(z=\tan\theta\gt 0\). Since \(a^2=u^2/(1+z^2)\), the trajectory becomes

\[\begin{gathered}y=y_0+(x-x_0)z\\\quad-\frac{g(x-x_0)^2}{2u^2}(1+z^2)\end{gathered}\]

The horizontal coordinate must lie in the actual free-flight segment. A parabola drawn beyond impact is an algebraic continuation, not the subsequent motion.

A target can give two launch angles

For fixed speed and a specified point, substitution produces a quadratic in \(z\). Find all real positive roots, then check the required flight interval. To compare arrival times, use \(t=(x-x_0)\sqrt{1+z^2}/u\). A larger angle can take longer and can be descending where the other trajectory is rising.

\[\begin{gathered}\frac{dy}{dx}=z-\frac{g(x-x_0)}{u^2}(1+z^2)\end{gathered}\]

For rightward motion the sign of this gradient identifies rising or falling. Alternatively evaluate the vertical velocity at the arrival time.

A wall is a set of allowed contact points

A vertical face of height \(h\) requires its horizontal coordinate and \(0\lt y\le h\) when top contact counts but ground contact does not. Combine this with any condition such as being later than a given point. Different wording changes the endpoints. For a finite inclined barrier, solve the line intersection and then check that its coordinate lies on the segment.

Clearance and optimisation are separate steps

First find the full angle interval that clears a wall; only then minimise or maximise the requested range over it. Compare endpoints and stationary values. If top contact is excluded, an endpoint value may be an unattained infimum. The formula \(R=u^2\sin2\theta/g\) assumes a return to the launch level.

Test reachability at the specified target

A negative discriminant for the target's angle equation means that point cannot be reached at the fixed speed. This conclusion needs no general envelope formula. If a discriminant is non-negative, positivity of \(z\) and the physical flight conditions still need checking.
lessons.method:
1. Derive the trajectory from the component equations with the actual initial position.
  2. Use the target, wall or given trajectory to obtain equations in the unknown settings.
  3. Find every admissible root or interval, preserving strict and inclusive endpoints.
  4. Check direction, arrival time and contact with any finite segment.
  5. For optimisation, use only the feasible settings and justify the endpoint or stationary choice.
mistakes: A trajectory starting above ground needs its initial-height term.
A fixed-speed target equation can have two valid positive angle roots.
The sign of the trajectory gradient needs the direction of horizontal travel.
The wall-top and ground-contact boundaries can have different inclusions.
A minimum over a feasible interval is not found by optimising over all angles.

examples.title: 1 · Keep the launch-height term
examples.question: A projectile starts at \((0,2)\) m with components \((10,15)\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). With \(g=10\), obtain its Cartesian trajectory and highest point.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}t=\frac x{10},\qquad y=2+15t-5t^2\\y=2+\frac32x-\frac{x^2}{20}\\\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac32-\frac x{10}=0\\(x_{\rm top},y_{\rm top})=\left(15,\frac{53}{4}\right)\end{gathered}\]

The same point is obtained at \(t=15/10\). The constant 2 records the height of the launch point.

examples.title: 2 · Both angles and both arrival times
examples.question: A particle is projected from the origin with speed \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). It must pass through \((20,10)\) m. With \(g=10\), find both acute launch angles and compare the arrival times and directions.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}10=20z-5(1+z^2),\qquad z=\tan\theta\\z^2-4z+3=0,\qquad z=1,3\\t=\sqrt{1+z^2}\\t=\sqrt2,\sqrt{10}\\\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{z=1}=0,\qquad\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{z=3}=-2\end{gathered}\]

The lower angle arrives first, at its highest point. The higher-angle shot is falling. Both reach a positive target height before their first ground return.

examples.title: 3 · A complete wall-position interval
examples.question: A projectile follows \(y=2x-\frac{x^2}{10}\), from \((0,0)\) towards increasing \(x\). After passing \((10,10)\), it strikes a vertical wall of height 6 m. Top contact counts; ground contact does not. Find all wall coordinates \(D\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}0\lt 2D-\frac{D^2}{10}\le6,\qquad D\gt 10\\y=6:\quad D=10\pm2\sqrt{10}\\y=0:\quad D=0,20\\10+2\sqrt{10}\le D\lt 20\end{gathered}\]

On the descending branch after \(x=10\), the height decreases. The smaller height-6 root is on the earlier rising branch and does not satisfy the stated order of events.

examples.title: 4 · A target that cannot be reached
examples.question: A launcher has fixed speed \(5\sqrt{10}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). With \(g=10\), decide whether any acute angle can reach \((20,15)\) m from the origin.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}15=20z-8(1+z^2)\\8z^2-20z+23=0\\\Delta=(-20)^2-4(8)(23)=-336\lt 0\end{gathered}\]

There is no real launch-angle tangent. Thus the target is inaccessible at this speed. This is a calculation for this point only, without an envelope formula.

lessons.title: Meetings, rebounds and release into free flight
lessons.summary: Use a common event, a separate clock for each stage and the correct transition conditions.
lessons.objective: Connect projectile segments without losing timing, velocity signs or the physical contact boundaries.
lessons.before: Complete components and trajectories. The rebound problems also use the coefficient of restitution. The string-cut problem additionally uses energy and radial force in circular motion; these prerequisites are summarised below and belong to later Mechanics chapters.
lessons.ideas:
One meeting instant can mean two elapsed times

Write a position equation for each object at the same physical instant. If the second launch occurs \(d\) seconds later and its elapsed time is \(s\), the first object has flown for \(s+d\). Set both coordinates equal and check that both objects are still in flight.

Equal gravitational accelerations cancel in a relative-position equation only when the time origins are handled correctly. A powered target maintaining height is not in free fall: use its stated motion rather than adding a gravitational drop.

Start a new clock after an impact

Position is continuous at the collision. The post-impact velocity becomes the initial velocity for a new projectile segment. For a fixed smooth plane, the tangential component stays unchanged while the signed normal component reverses and is multiplied by the coefficient \(e\), with \(0\le e\le1\):

\[\begin{gathered}v_{\parallel}^{+}=v_{\parallel}^{-},\qquad v_{\perp}^{+}=-e v_{\perp}^{-}\end{gathered}\]

A vertical wall changes horizontal velocity only; a horizontal platform changes vertical velocity only. For an inclined wall at angle \(\phi\), resolve along the wall and a chosen perpendicular, apply the two rules and resolve back:

\[\begin{gathered}p=v_x\cos\phi+v_y\sin\phi\\n=-v_x\sin\phi+v_y\cos\phi\\v_x^+=p\cos\phi+en\sin\phi\\v_y^+=p\sin\phi-en\cos\phi\end{gathered}\]

Keep signed components through this calculation. Restitution scales the normal component, not the entire speed. For a finite barrier, a later intersection with its infinite line is another impact only if it lies on the actual segment.

Release from a circle starts a projectile, not another circular arc

Immediately after a deliberate cut, velocity is tangent to the circle and is continuous. The launch position is the cut point. Gravity then supplies the free-flight acceleration; tension is zero after the cut. For radius vector \((X,Y)\) of length \(a\), a left-and-up unit tangent on the upper-right arc is \((-Y/a,X/a)\).

Check the pre-release circular motion separately

For a particle attached by a light string, measured relative to the circle centre, conservation of energy relates the speed \(w\) at the bottom to the speed \(v\) at height \(y\). The radial equation gives the tension \(\mathcal T\):

\[\begin{gathered}v^2=w^2-2g(y+a)\\\mathcal T=\frac{mv^2}{a}-\frac{mgy}{a}\\\mathcal T=\frac{mw^2}{a}-2mg-\frac{3mgy}{a}\end{gathered}\]

Along the rising arc this tension decreases with height, so its value just before the cut is the minimum over that arc. A string cannot supply compression: establish non-negative tension throughout. A deliberate cut does not require zero tension beforehand.

Finish with physical consistency

Check every meeting or contact occurs before first landing. Distinguish horizontal distance travelled from signed displacement after a leftward rebound. A second root belonging to a different stage or to a line extension is not automatically a physical event.
lessons.method:
1. Draw or describe the objects, stages, axes and common event.
  2. Give each flight its own elapsed time and write both component equations.
  3. At a collision or release, retain position and determine the new signed velocity.
  4. Solve the next segment and check all ground, segment and string constraints.
  5. State distance or displacement as requested, with exact values and units.
mistakes: Delayed launches have different elapsed flight times at the meeting.
A powered target holding height does not acquire a free-fall vertical displacement.
Restitution applies to the normal component, not the whole velocity.
The cut-point height is not automatically the ground or the circle centre.
A line-extension crossing or negative tension can invalidate a proposed event.

examples.title: 1 · A later launch uses a shorter clock
examples.question: From a point 40 m above ground, \(P\) is launched with components \((12,18)\). One second later \(Q\) is launched from the same point. They meet two seconds after \(Q\) starts. With \(g=10\), find the initial components of \(Q\) and the meeting height.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}P:\quad t=3,\quad(x,y)=(36,9)\\Q:\quad 2a=36,\qquad2b-5(2)^2=9\\a=18,\qquad b=\frac{29}{2}\\h_{\rm meet}=40+9=49\end{gathered}\]

The two particles have flown for 3 s and 2 s. Both begin above ground and meet above ground; concavity of their height functions rules out an earlier landing.

examples.title: 2 · A powered target does not fall
examples.question: A target stays 18 m high and moves left at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), starting 44 m to the right of the origin. A ball is launched from the origin at the same instant, with \(\tan\theta=\frac{19}{18}\). With \(g=10\), find its initial speed and interception time.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}x_{\rm target}=44-4t,\qquad y_{\rm target}=18\\x_{\rm ball}=at,\qquad y_{\rm ball}=\frac{19}{18}at-5t^2\\18=\frac{19}{18}(44-4t)-5t^2\\(t-2)(45t+128)=0\\t=2,\quad a=18,\quad b=19,\quad u=\sqrt{685}\end{gathered}\]

Discard the negative time. At interception the ball has vertical component \(-1\), so it is just descending; the target still has zero vertical velocity because its height is actively maintained.

examples.title: 3 · Resolve the rebound, then restart the flight
examples.question: A ball reaches a smooth vertical wall at height 12 m with velocity \((10,-2)\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The restitution coefficient is \(3/5\). With \(g=10\), find its post-impact velocity and horizontal distance travelled before ground contact.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}v_x^+=-\frac35(10)=-6,\qquad v_y^+=-2\\y=12-2s-5s^2\\s=\frac{\sqrt{61}-1}{5}\\\text{horizontal distance}=\frac{6(\sqrt{61}-1)}5\end{gathered}\]

Here \(s\) is time since impact. The leftward displacement has the negative of this distance. As the ball moves away from a vertical wall with constant negative horizontal component, it cannot hit the same wall again during this segment.

examples.title: 4 · A cut preserves tangential velocity
examples.question: A particle moves up the right-hand side of a circle of radius \(a\), on a string fixed at its centre. The string is cut at \((\frac{3a}{5},\frac{4a}{5})\), with left-and-up tangent speed \(V\). Its subsequent flight passes through \((0,a)\). Find \(V^2\) and check whether the preceding arc from the bottom can have a taut string.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}(v_x,v_y)=\left(-\frac45V,\frac35V\right)\\t=\frac{3a}{4V},\qquad\frac a5=\frac35Vt-\frac12gt^2\\V^2=\frac98ag\\w^2=V^2+\frac{18}{5}ag=\frac{189}{40}ag\\\mathcal T_B=\frac{229}{40}mg,\qquad\mathcal T_D=\frac{13}{40}mg\gt 0\end{gathered}\]

Energy uses the rise \(\frac{9a}{5}\) from the bottom to the cut. Tension decreases along that rising arc, so its positive value just before the cut proves the string can stay taut throughout. Immediately afterwards the motion is a projectile; the old circular force equation no longer applies.

questions.title: Meeting during the downward journey
questions.prompt_html:
Throughout free flight, neglect air resistance and take the acceleration due to gravity to be \(g\), vertically downwards.

Two particles start simultaneously in the same vertical plane. Particle \(P\) starts at \(O\); particle \(Q\) starts at a point vertically above \(O\), a distance \(d\) away. Both have a horizontal component of velocity to the right. Particle \(P\) is projected with speed \(U\) at an angle \(\alpha\) above the horizontal, while \(Q\) is projected with speed \(V\) at an angle \(\beta\) below it, where \(0\lt \alpha,\beta\lt 90^\circ\). They meet after time \(T\).

  1. Eliminate \(V\) to express \(d\) in terms of \(U,T,\alpha\) and \(\beta\).

    [3]

  2. Now \(\tan\alpha=3/4\) and \(\tan\beta=5/12\). At the meeting point, the vertical component of the velocity of \(P\) is \(U/5\) downwards. Find \(T,V\) and \(d\) in terms of \(U\) and \(g\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(d=UT(\sin\alpha+\cos\alpha\tan\beta)\).

(b)

\(T=4U/(5g),\ V=13U/15,\ d=56U^2/(75g)\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The horizontal displacements at the meeting point are equal, so \(U\cos\alpha\,T=V\cos\beta\,T\). Since \(T\gt 0\), \(V\cos\beta=U\cos\alpha\).

Taking upward as positive, equality of vertical positions gives

\[U\sin\alpha\,T-\frac12gT^2=d-V\sin\beta\,T-\frac12gT^2.\]

The two gravitational terms cancel. Therefore \(d=T(U\sin\alpha+V\sin\beta)\). Substituting \(V=U\cos\alpha/\cos\beta\) gives

\[d=UT(\sin\alpha+\cos\alpha\tan\beta).\]

Part (b)

The angle data give \(\sin\alpha=3/5,\ \cos\alpha=4/5,\ \sin\beta=5/13\) and \(\cos\beta=12/13\).

At the meeting point, \(3U/5-gT=-U/5\), so \(T=4U/(5g)\). Equality of the horizontal velocities gives \((12/13)V=(4/5)U\), hence \(V=13U/15\).

Finally,

\[d=\frac{4U^2}{5g}\left(\frac35+\frac45\frac5{12}\right)=\frac{56U^2}{75g}.\]

As a physical check, the meeting point is \(4U^2/(25g)\) above \(O\); the lower particle is still above its launch level.
questions.hint_html: Compare positions, not distances travelled. The gravitational terms cancel when both particles are compared at the same time.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the signed downward component to obtain the time.

questions.title: Recovering a restitution coefficient
questions.prompt_html:
Throughout free flight, neglect air resistance and take the acceleration due to gravity to be \(g\), vertically downwards.

A small smooth ball is launched from \(O\) with speed \(U\), at an angle \(\alpha\) above the horizontal where \(\tan\alpha=3/4\). It strikes a smooth horizontal platform below \(O\). Immediately before impact its direction of motion makes an angle \(\tan^{-1}2\) below the horizontal. Immediately after impact it moves at \(45^\circ\) above the horizontal. Write \(T\) for the time to impact, \(D\) for the horizontal displacement and \(H\) for the vertical drop from \(O\) to the platform.

  1. Write down the horizontal and upward vertical components of the velocity at time \(t\), before impact.

    [2]

  2. Find \(T\).

    [3]

  3. Find the ratio \(H:D\).

    [3]

  4. Find the coefficient of restitution and the speed immediately after impact.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(v_x=4U/5,\quad v_y=3U/5-gt\).

(b)

\(T=11U/(5g)\).

(c)

\(H:D=5:8\).

(d)

\(e=1/2\), and the rebound speed is \(4\sqrt2\,U/5\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

There is no horizontal acceleration. Resolving the initial velocity and using upward as positive gives

\[v_x=U\cos\alpha=\frac45U,\qquad v_y=U\sin\alpha-gt=\frac35U-gt.\]

Part (b)

At impact, the downward component is twice the horizontal component. Thus \(v_y=-8U/5\), not \(+8U/5\).

\[\frac35U-gT=-\frac85U\quad\Longrightarrow\quad T=\frac{11U}{5g}.\]

Part (c)

Horizontal motion gives

\[D=\frac45U\,T=\frac{44U^2}{25g}.\]

Since the vertical displacement is \(-H\),

\[H=\frac12gT^2-\frac35UT=\frac{121U^2}{50g}-\frac{33U^2}{25g}=\frac{11U^2}{10g}.\]

Consequently \(H/D=5/8\), so \(H:D=5:8\).

Part (d)

For a smooth horizontal platform the horizontal component is unchanged. The normal component is vertical; it reverses direction and its magnitude is multiplied by \(e\).

After impact the components are \(4U/5\) and \(8eU/5\). The rebound angle is \(45^\circ\), so these are equal. Hence \(e=1/2\).

\[w=\sqrt{\left(\frac45U\right)^2+\left(\frac45U\right)^2}=\frac{4\sqrt2}{5}U.\]
questions.hint_html: The angle before impact determines a signed vertical velocity. Restitution changes the normal component only.

questions.title: Two launch speeds from a raised platform
questions.prompt_html:
Throughout free flight, neglect air resistance and take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), vertically downwards.

A particle is launched from a point \(50\) m above horizontal ground with speed \(u\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Its initial direction makes an angle \(\theta\) above the horizontal, where \(\tan\theta=2\). Its directions of motion at \(t=1\) s and \(t=4\) s are perpendicular.

  1. Find all possible values of \(u\), checking that the particle has not reached the ground at either stated time.

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(u=10(\sqrt5+1)\) or \(u=10(\sqrt5-1)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\); both are valid.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The horizontal component is \(u/\sqrt5\gt 0\), and the vertical component is \(2u/\sqrt5-10t\). The gradients of the two directions therefore have product \(-1\):

\[\left(\frac{2u/\sqrt5-10}{u/\sqrt5}\right)\left(\frac{2u/\sqrt5-40}{u/\sqrt5}\right)=-1.\]

After multiplication and simplification,

\[u^2-20\sqrt5\,u+400=0.\]

The discriminant is \(400\), giving \(u=10(\sqrt5\pm1)\); both values are positive.

At \(t=4\), height above the ground is

\[50+\frac{8u}{\sqrt5}-80=50\pm16\sqrt5.\]

Both heights are positive because \(16\sqrt5\lt 50\). Height is a concave quadratic and is positive at both ends of \([0,4]\), so it stays above ground throughout this interval. Neither root is to be discarded.
questions.hint_html: For perpendicular non-vertical directions, the product of their gradients is \(-1\). Check height above the actual ground, not above the launch point.

marking_criteria.description_html: Verify that both trajectories are above ground for the observations.

questions.title: A speed ratio and a right-angle turn
questions.prompt_html:
Throughout free flight, neglect air resistance and take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), vertically downwards.

A particle is projected from horizontal ground with speed \(u\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at angle \(\theta\), where \(0\lt \theta\lt 90^\circ\). Three seconds later its speed is \(5u/12\), and its direction of motion is perpendicular to its initial direction.

  1. Derive an equation relating \(u\) and \(\sin\theta\) from the speed information.

    [3]

  2. Find \(u\) and \(\sin\theta\).

    [4]

  3. Check that the observation at three seconds is made before the particle reaches the ground.

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\frac{119}{144}u^2-60u\sin\theta+900=0\).

(b)

\(u=360/13\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), \(\sin\theta=12/13\).

(c)

The flight time is \(864/169\) s, which exceeds \(3\) s.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

After three seconds the horizontal and vertical components are \(u\cos\theta\) and \(u\sin\theta-30\). Squaring and adding,

\[(u\cos\theta)^2+(u\sin\theta-30)^2=\frac{25}{144}u^2.\]

Use \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1\) and collect terms to obtain

\[\frac{119}{144}u^2-60u\sin\theta+900=0.\]

Part (b)

The initial gradient is \(\tan\theta\); the later gradient must be \(-\cot\theta\). Therefore

\[\frac{u\sin\theta-30}{u\cos\theta}=-\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}.\]

Multiplying by \(u\sin\theta\cos\theta\) gives \(u=30\sin\theta\). In the equation from (a), substitute \(u\sin\theta=u^2/30\):

\[\left(\frac{119}{144}-2\right)u^2+900=0.\]

Thus \(u^2=129600/169\). Taking the positive root gives \(u=360/13\), and then \(\sin\theta=12/13\).

Part (c)

The time to return to ground is

\[\frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}=\frac{2(360/13)(12/13)}{10}=\frac{864}{169}\gt 3.\]

The stated observation is therefore within the flight.
questions.hint_html: Use separate equations for speed and direction. A downward velocity component is not a negative speed.

Compare the observation time with the correct total flight time.

questions.title: Descent measured from the highest point
questions.prompt_html:
Throughout free flight, neglect air resistance and take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), vertically downwards.

A particle is projected from horizontal ground with speed \(30\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at angle \(\theta\), where \(0\lt \theta\lt 90^\circ\). Its greatest height is \(H\) metres and it reaches that height at time \(T\) seconds. By time \(t=4\) s, it is descending and has fallen through \(4H/9\) from the highest point.

  1. Express \(T\) and \(H\) in terms of \(\theta\).

    [3]

  2. Find \(\theta\).

    [3]

  3. Find the speed and direction of motion at \(t=4\) s.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(T=3\sin\theta\), \(H=45\sin^2\theta\).

(b)

\(\theta=\sin^{-1}(4/5)\approx53.1^\circ\).

(c)

\(2\sqrt{145}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), at \(\tan^{-1}(8/9)\approx41.6^\circ\) below the horizontal.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

At the top, the vertical velocity is zero. Hence \(0=30\sin\theta-10T\), so \(T=3\sin\theta\).

Using vertical motion from launch to the top,

\[0=(30\sin\theta)^2-20H\quad\Longrightarrow\quad H=45\sin^2\theta.\]

Equivalently, since the upward component is \(10T\), \(H=5T^2\).

Part (b)

The descent starts from zero vertical velocity. Its duration is \(4-T\gt 0\), so

\[5(4-T)^2=\frac49H=\frac{20}{9}T^2.\]

Both durations are positive; therefore \(4-T=2T/3\), not the negative square root. This gives \(T=12/5\). Consequently \(\sin\theta=T/3=4/5\), and \(\theta\approx53.1^\circ\).

Part (c)

Since \(\cos\theta=3/5\), the horizontal velocity is \(18\). The vertical velocity at four seconds is \(24-40=-16\).

\[v=\sqrt{18^2+(-16)^2}=2\sqrt{145}.\]

The downward direction makes angle \(\tan^{-1}(16/18)=\tan^{-1}(8/9)\) with the horizontal. The particle remains above ground because its total flight time is \(2T=24/5\gt 4\).
questions.hint_html: From the highest point, the initial vertical velocity is zero. Use \(4-T\) for the descending time.

questions.title: Intercepting an approaching target
questions.prompt_html:
Throughout free flight, neglect air resistance and take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), vertically downwards.

At time zero a powered target is at height \(16\) m and horizontal distance \(56\) m to the right of \(O\). It travels horizontally towards \(O\) at a constant speed of \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), maintaining its height. At that same instant a ball is projected from \(O\) with speed \(u\) at angle \(\theta\) above the horizontal, where \(\tan\theta=3/4\). The ball and target meet. Treat both objects as particles.

  1. Find the time of interception and the initial speed of the ball.

    [5]

  2. Find the direction of motion of the ball immediately before interception.

    [3]

  3. Explain why the target height must not be modelled by \(16-5t^2\).

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(T=2\) s and \(u=30\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

(b)

\(\tan^{-1}(1/12)\approx4.76^\circ\) below the horizontal.

(c)

The target is powered and maintains constant height; it is not in free fall.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Using \(\cos\theta=4/5\) and \(\sin\theta=3/5\), equality of horizontal coordinates gives

\[\frac45uT=56-4T.\]

The target remains at height 16, so the ball satisfies

\[\frac35uT-5T^2=16.\]

Multiply the first equation by \(3/4\) and substitute into the second:

\[42-3T-5T^2=16.\]

Thus \(5T^2+3T-26=(T-2)(5T+13)=0\). Reject \(T=-13/5\), since the interception occurs after launch. Hence \(T=2\), and the horizontal equation then gives \(u=30\).

Part (b)

At interception the horizontal component is \((4/5)30=24\), and the upward component is \((3/5)30-10(2)=-2\).

The angle below the horizontal is \(\tan^{-1}(2/24)=\tan^{-1}(1/12)\), approximately \(4.76^\circ\).

Part (c)

The target is specified to move at constant height, so its vertical acceleration is zero. Its propulsion supplies the force needed to balance its weight. The equation \(16-5t^2\) would instead describe an unpowered particle released with zero vertical velocity.
questions.hint_html: The target approaches the launch point, so its horizontal coordinate decreases. Its vertical coordinate is constant.

questions.title: A delayed launch from a cliff
questions.prompt_html:
Throughout free flight, neglect air resistance and take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), vertically downwards.

A launch point \(O\) is \(45\) m vertically above level ground. Particle \(P\) is projected from \(O\) with horizontal velocity \(15\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) to the right and vertical velocity \(25/2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) upwards. One second later, particle \(Q\) is projected from \(O\), also to the right, with speed \(u\) and angle \(\beta\), where \(\tan\beta=1/4\). They meet \(T\) seconds after \(Q\) is launched.

  1. Write equations for equality of the horizontal and vertical coordinates at the meeting point.

    [3]

  2. Find \(T\) and \(u\).

    [4]

  3. Find the horizontal and vertical displacements of the meeting point from \(O\), with signs stated.

    [3]

  4. Check that the meeting occurs above the ground.

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(15(T+1)=4uT/\sqrt{17}\); \(\frac{25}{2}(T+1)-5(T+1)^2=uT/\sqrt{17}-5T^2\).

(b)

\(T=3\) s and \(u=5\sqrt{17}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

(c)

\(60\) m right and \(30\) m down: \((x,y)=(60,-30)\) m.

(d)

The meeting height is \(45-30=15\) m above ground.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Use the same meeting instant but different elapsed flight times: \(P\) has flown for \(T+1\) seconds and \(Q\) for \(T\) seconds. Also \(\cos\beta=4/\sqrt{17}\) and \(\sin\beta=1/\sqrt{17}\).

Relative to \(O\), equality of horizontal and vertical coordinates gives

\[15(T+1)=\frac{4uT}{\sqrt{17}},\]
\[\frac{25}{2}(T+1)-5(T+1)^2=\frac{uT}{\sqrt{17}}-5T^2.\]

Part (b)

The horizontal equation gives \(uT/\sqrt{17}=15(T+1)/4\). Substitute this into the vertical equation:

\[\frac{35}{4}(T+1)-5\big((T+1)^2-T^2\big)=0.\]

Multiplying by 4 gives \(35(T+1)-20(2T+1)=0\), hence \(T=3\).

Using the horizontal equation again, \(60=12u/\sqrt{17}\), so \(u=5\sqrt{17}\).

Part (c)

Particle \(P\) has been in flight for 4 seconds, so

\[x=15(4)=60,\qquad y=\frac{25}{2}(4)-5(4)^2=-30.\]

As a check, \(Q\) has initial components 20 and 5; after 3 seconds its coordinates are also \((60,15-45)=(60,-30)\).

Part (d)

The reference point \(O\) is 45 m above ground. A displacement of \(-30\) m from \(O\) therefore leaves a height of 15 m. Both free-flight paths are concave height functions with positive heights at launch and meeting, so neither particle has already hit the ground.
questions.hint_html: At the common meeting instant, one particle has been moving for one second longer. Do not cancel the two gravitational terms without expanding their different times.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the two correct elapsed flight times.
State the direction or the signed coordinate convention.
Compare the displacement with the given cliff height.

questions.title: Recovering a trajectory from one speed reading
questions.prompt_html:
Throughout free flight, neglect air resistance and take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), vertically downwards.

A particle is launched from level ground with speed \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at an acute angle \(\theta\) above the horizontal. At \(t=2\) s its speed is \(8\sqrt5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

  1. Find \(\sin\theta\).

    [3]

  2. Find the horizontal range before the particle first returns to the ground.

    [3]

  3. Find the minimum speed during this flight and the time at which it occurs.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\sin\theta=3/5\).

(b)

\(R=192/5\) m.

(c)

\(16\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), at \(t=6/5\) s.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

At two seconds the components are \(20\cos\theta\) and \(20\sin\theta-20\). Hence

\[(20\cos\theta)^2+(20\sin\theta-20)^2=320.\]

Simplifying gives \(800-800\sin\theta=320\), so \(\sin\theta=3/5\). The acute-angle condition gives \(\cos\theta=4/5\).

Part (b)

The initial components are 16 horizontally and 12 vertically. At return to ground,

\[0=12t-5t^2=t(12-5t).\]

The nonzero flight time is \(12/5\) s. The range is therefore \(16(12/5)=192/5\) m.

Part (c)

At time \(t\), \(v^2=16^2+(12-10t)^2\). This is smallest when the vertical component is zero, at \(t=6/5\) s. The horizontal component remains 16, so the minimum speed is 16, not zero.
questions.hint_html: Use speed squared to recover the launch component. The particle does not stop at the top: only its vertical velocity is zero.

marking_criteria.description_html: Set the vertical displacement equal to zero.
Identify zero vertical velocity as the minimum-speed condition.
Give the correct time and minimum speed.

questions.title: A rebound that lands short of the wall
questions.prompt_html:
Throughout free flight, neglect air resistance and take the acceleration due to gravity to be \(g\), vertically downwards.

A ball is launched from a point \(O\) on level ground with speed \(U\), at an angle \(\alpha\) where \(\tan\alpha=3/2\). A sufficiently high, smooth vertical wall stands 18 m to the right of \(O\). The ball strikes the wall and then lands on the ground at a point 6 m to the right of \(O\). The coefficient of restitution between the ball and the wall is \(1/2\).

  1. Find the total time of flight \(\tau\) in terms of \(U\) and \(g\).

    [2]

  2. Explain why this time is the same as it would be without the wall.

    [2]

  3. Find \(U^2\) in terms of \(g\).

    [4]

  4. Determine whether the ball is rising or falling when it strikes the wall.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\tau=6U/(g\sqrt{13})\).

(b)

A smooth vertical wall changes only horizontal velocity; vertical position and velocity are continuous through the impact.

(c)

\(U^2=91g/2\), in SI units.

(d)

It is rising: the wall is reached at \(3\tau/7\lt \tau/2\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The initial vertical component is \(3U/\sqrt{13}\). Returning to the original ground level requires

\[0=\frac{3U}{\sqrt{13}}\tau-\frac12g\tau^2.\]

Taking the nonzero root gives \(\tau=6U/(g\sqrt{13})\).

Part (b)

The impulse from a smooth vertical wall is horizontal. Therefore the vertical velocity does not change at impact, and the vertical motion continues to follow the same equation from the original launch. The first return to ground consequently occurs at the same time.

Part (c)

Let \(a=2U/\sqrt{13}\) be the initial horizontal velocity. The time to the wall is \(18/a\). After impact the horizontal velocity is \(-a/2\). Hence the landing coordinate is

\[6=18-\frac a2\left(\tau-\frac{18}{a}\right)=27-\frac{a\tau}{2}.\]

It follows that \(a\tau=42\). But

\[a\tau=\frac{2U}{\sqrt{13}}\frac{6U}{g\sqrt{13}}=\frac{12U^2}{13g}.\]

Thus \(12U^2/(13g)=42\), giving \(U^2=91g/2\).

Part (d)

The wall time is \(t_w=18/a\), so \(t_w/\tau=18/(a\tau)=18/42=3/7\). The highest point occurs at \(\tau/2\). Therefore impact occurs before the highest point, while the ball is rising. Its impact height is \(108/7\) m, so a wall exceeding this height suffices.
questions.hint_html: Write the horizontal displacement as a forward part followed by a backward part. It is not the total distance travelled.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the vertical equation for return to launch level.
Connect this to the unchanged return time.
Relate the unrestricted horizontal range to the speed.
Compare wall time with the flight time or apex time.
State and justify that the ball is rising.

questions.title: Two crossings of the same height
questions.prompt_html:
Throughout free flight, neglect air resistance and take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), vertically downwards.

A particle is launched from horizontal ground with speed \(50\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), at angle \(\theta\) where \(\tan\theta=3/4\). It crosses a horizontal level of height \(H\) twice during its flight. The two crossing times differ by four seconds.

  1. Find the two crossing times and the value of \(H\).

    [5]

  2. Find the speed and direction of the particle half a second before it first returns to the ground.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

The crossings are at \(t=1\) s and \(t=5\) s; \(H=25\) m.

(b)

\(5\sqrt{89}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), at \(\tan^{-1}(5/8)\approx32.0^\circ\) below the horizontal.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The initial components are \(40\) horizontally and \(30\) vertically. Thus the height is \(y=30t-5t^2\). Setting \(y=H\) gives

\[5t^2-30t+H=0.\]

If the roots are \(t_1\lt t_2\), their sum is 6, while \(t_2-t_1=4\). Solving gives \(t_1=1\), \(t_2=5\). Substitution into the height equation yields \(H=30-5=25\) m.

Both times lie between launch and the ground-return time \(6\) s.

Part (b)

The total flight time is \(2(30)/10=6\) s, so the required time is \(11/2\) s. The components are

\[v_x=40,\qquad v_y=30-10\left(\frac{11}{2}\right)=-25.\]

The speed is \(\sqrt{40^2+25^2}=5\sqrt{89}\). The direction is \(\tan^{-1}(25/40)=\tan^{-1}(5/8)\), about \(32.0^\circ\) below the horizontal.
questions.hint_html: The two visits to a horizontal level are symmetric in time about the highest point.

marking_criteria.description_html: Obtain the initial vertical component and height equation.
Use the sum of the two roots or symmetry about the apex.
Combine with the difference of the times.
Find the correct time before ground impact.

questions.title: Rejecting a speed that lands too early
questions.prompt_html:
Throughout free flight, neglect air resistance and take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), vertically downwards.

A particle is launched from level ground with speed \(u\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at angle \(\theta\), where \(\tan\theta=4/3\). It moves freely until its first return to the ground; no rebound is considered. The directions of its motion at \(t=1\) s and \(t=9\) s, both during that flight, are perpendicular.

  1. Find \(u\). Explain why any other positive root obtained algebraically is inadmissible.

    [7]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(u=40+10\sqrt7\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The smaller root \(40-10\sqrt7\) returns to the ground before \(t=9\) s.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The horizontal velocity is \(3u/5\), and the vertical velocity is \(4u/5-10t\). Since the two direction gradients have product \(-1\),

\[\left(\frac{4u/5-10}{3u/5}\right)\left(\frac{4u/5-90}{3u/5}\right)=-1.\]

Multiplying out gives \(u^2-80u+900=0\), hence

\[u=40\pm10\sqrt7.\]

A positive algebraic root is not automatically a valid physical solution. The first return to ground occurs at

\[t_f=\frac{2(4u/5)}{10}=\frac{4u}{25}.\]

For the smaller root, \(t_f=(32-8\sqrt7)/5\approx2.17\) s, which is less than 9 s. That root contradicts the observation being made during the first flight.

For the larger root, \(t_f=(32+8\sqrt7)/5\approx10.63\) s, so both observations are valid. Therefore \(u=40+10\sqrt7\).
questions.hint_html: First solve the perpendicular-direction equation. Then test each root against the requirement that the first flight lasts longer than nine seconds.

marking_criteria.description_html: Obtain the total flight time in terms of the speed.
Reject the smaller root by a time comparison.

questions.title: When is the right-angle direction reached in the air?
questions.prompt_html:
Throughout free flight, neglect air resistance and take the acceleration due to gravity to be \(g\), vertically downwards.

A particle is projected from level ground with speed \(u\gt 0\) at angle \(\alpha\), where \(0\lt \alpha\lt 90^\circ\). The time at which its direction of motion is perpendicular to its initial direction is denoted by \(T\), whenever this occurs before the first impact with the ground.

  1. Obtain an expression for \(T\).

    [2]

  2. Find the exact set of launch angles for which this event occurs strictly before ground impact. Explain what happens at the lower boundary.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(T=u/(g\sin\alpha)\).

(b)

\(45^\circ\lt \alpha\lt 90^\circ\). At \(\alpha=45^\circ\), the event occurs at ground impact, not while strictly airborne.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The later direction gradient is \((u\sin\alpha-gT)/(u\cos\alpha)\). The gradient perpendicular to the initial direction is \(-\cot\alpha\). Thus

\[\frac{u\sin\alpha-gT}{u\cos\alpha}=-\frac{\cos\alpha}{\sin\alpha}.\]

Multiplying and using \(\sin^2\alpha+\cos^2\alpha=1\) gives \(u=gT\sin\alpha\). Hence \(T=u/(g\sin\alpha)\).

Part (b)

The first ground-return time is \(t_f=2u\sin\alpha/g\). The required strict inequality is

\[\frac{u}{g\sin\alpha}\lt \frac{2u\sin\alpha}{g}.\]

All cancelled quantities are positive, so this is equivalent to \(\sin^2\alpha\gt 1/2\). On the stated acute-angle interval this gives \(\alpha\gt 45^\circ\), and therefore \(45^\circ\lt \alpha\lt 90^\circ\).

At \(45^\circ\) the two times are equal. A perpendicular direction exists at the instant of impact, but not strictly earlier. For smaller angles the algebraic time lies after landing and is not part of this flight.
questions.hint_html: An algebraic time obtained from velocity formulas must lie within the physical interval of free flight.

marking_criteria.description_html: Compare with the correct total flight time.

questions.title: Velocity after the apex
questions.prompt_html:
Throughout free flight, neglect air resistance and take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), vertically downwards.

A particle is projected with speed \(u\) at angle \(\theta\) where \(\tan\theta=5/12\). It starts on horizontal ground. Its highest point is reached at time \(T\).

  1. Find the speed at time \(7T/5\), in terms of \(u\).

    [3]

  2. Find the direction of motion at that time.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(2\sqrt{37}\,u/13\).

(b)

\(\tan^{-1}(1/6)\approx9.46^\circ\) below the horizontal.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The initial components are \(12u/13\) and \(5u/13\). At the top, \(gT=5u/13\). Therefore at \(t=7T/5\),

\[v_y=\frac{5u}{13}-\frac75gT=\frac{5u}{13}-\frac{7u}{13}=-\frac{2u}{13}.\]

The horizontal component remains \(12u/13\). Hence

\[v=\frac{u}{13}\sqrt{12^2+2^2}=\frac{2\sqrt{37}}{13}u.\]

Part (b)

The vertical component is negative, so the particle is descending. Its angle below the horizontal is \(\tan^{-1}((2u/13)/(12u/13))=\tan^{-1}(1/6)\).

The time \(7T/5\) lies between the apex time \(T\) and the landing time \(2T\), as required.
questions.hint_html: Express \(gT\) using the vertical velocity at the top, before substituting the requested fraction of \(T\).

marking_criteria.description_html: Relate the apex time to the initial vertical component.
Obtain the later vertical and horizontal components.
Use the ratio of the component magnitudes.
Give the correct angle and downward direction.

questions.title: Two directions at a fraction of the maximum height
questions.prompt_html:
Throughout free flight, neglect air resistance and take the acceleration due to gravity to be \(g\), vertically downwards.

A particle is launched from level ground with speed \(u\) at acute angle \(\theta\). Its maximum height is \(H\). For a fixed number \(f\) with \(0\lt f\lt 1\), it crosses the level \(y=fH\) once upwards and once downwards.

  1. If its direction on the upward crossing makes angle \(\alpha\) above the horizontal, show that \(\tan\alpha=\sqrt{1-f}\tan\theta\).

    [3]

  2. Now \(f=9/25\) and \(\tan\theta=5/12\). Find the horizontal distance between the two crossings in terms of \(u\) and \(g\).

    [4]

  3. Let \(\gamma\) be the smaller angle between the directions of motion at the two crossings. Show that \(\tan\gamma=3/4\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\tan\alpha=\sqrt{1-f}\tan\theta\).

(b)

\(96u^2/(169g)\).

(c)

\(\gamma=2\tan^{-1}(1/3)\) and \(\tan\gamma=3/4\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The maximum height satisfies \(2gH=u^2\sin^2\theta\). At height \(fH\), vertical motion gives

\[v_y^2=u^2\sin^2\theta-2gfH=u^2\sin^2\theta(1-f).\]

On the upward crossing choose the positive root: \(v_y=u\sin\theta\sqrt{1-f}\). Divide by the constant horizontal component \(u\cos\theta\) to obtain \(\tan\alpha=\sqrt{1-f}\tan\theta\).

Part (b)

Here \(\sqrt{1-f}=4/5\), and the initial vertical component is \(5u/13\). The two vertical velocities are therefore \(\pm4u/13\).

From \(v_y=5u/13-gt\), the crossing times are

\[t_1=\frac{u}{13g},\qquad t_2=\frac{9u}{13g}.\]

The horizontal component is \(12u/13\), so the horizontal separation is

\[\Delta x=\frac{12u}{13}(t_2-t_1)=\frac{12u}{13}\frac{8u}{13g}=\frac{96u^2}{169g}.\]

Part (c)

The two directions are inclined at equal and opposite angles to the horizontal. From part (a), \(\tan\alpha=(4/5)(5/12)=1/3\).

Thus \(\gamma=2\alpha\). Since \(0\lt \alpha\lt 45^\circ\), this is the smaller angle and is acute. Using the double-angle formula,

\[\tan\gamma=\frac{2\tan\alpha}{1-\tan^2\alpha}=\frac{2/3}{1-1/9}=\frac34.\]
questions.hint_html: At equal heights the vertical components have equal magnitudes and opposite signs. The horizontal component is unchanged.

marking_criteria.description_html: Relate maximum height to the initial vertical component.
Find the vertical velocity at the stated height and select the upward sign.
Obtain both crossing times or their difference.
Identify the equal and opposite directional angles.
Obtain the value with the appropriate angle range.

questions.title: Oblique impact with a finite inclined barrier
questions.prompt_html:
Throughout free flight, neglect air resistance and take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), vertically downwards.

A ball is launched from \(O=(0,0)\) with horizontal component \(12\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) to the right and vertical component \(21\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) upwards. A smooth, fixed, thin barrier is the line segment joining \((34,16)\) to \((38,20)\), with coordinates in metres. Thus it slopes upwards to the right at \(45^\circ\). The ball strikes it at \(A\), when its downward vertical speed is \(9\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The coefficient of restitution is \(1/3\). After the impact it eventually reaches the ground \(y=0\).

  1. Find the time of impact and the coordinates of \(A\).

    [3]

  2. Find the speed immediately before impact.

    [2]

  3. Find the horizontal and vertical components of velocity immediately after impact.

    [4]

  4. Find the horizontal distance travelled after impact before the ball reaches the ground. Confirm that it does not strike the finite barrier again.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(t=3\) s and \(A=(36,18)\) m.

(b)

\(15\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

(c)

\(v_x=-2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), \(v_y=5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

(d)

\((5+\sqrt{385})/5\) m. The second intersection with the extended line is outside the barrier.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The downward velocity condition is \(21-10t=-9\), giving \(t=3\) s. Therefore

\[x=12(3)=36,\qquad y=21(3)-5(3)^2=18.\]

This point lies on the given segment, whose equation is \(y=x-18\) for \(34\le x\le38\). In fact solving the trajectory intersection gives the only positive intersection time \(t=3\), so there is no earlier impact.

Part (b)

Immediately before impact the components are 12 and \(-9\), so

\[v=\sqrt{12^2+(-9)^2}=\sqrt{225}=15\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}.\]

Part (c)

Resolve parallel to the barrier upwards-right, and normal to it upwards-left. Before impact the components are

\[v_{\parallel}=\frac{12-9}{\sqrt2}=\frac3{\sqrt2},\qquad v_{\perp}=\frac{-12-9}{\sqrt2}=-\frac{21}{\sqrt2}.\]

The smooth surface leaves the parallel component unchanged. Restitution gives the new normal component \(-(1/3)(-21/\sqrt2)=7/\sqrt2\).

Resolving back to horizontal and vertical,

\[v_x=\frac{3-7}{2}=-2,\qquad v_y=\frac{3+7}{2}=5.\]

The ball therefore moves leftwards and upwards just after impact.

Part (d)

Let \(s\) be time measured from impact. The rebound path is

\[x=36-2s,\qquad y=18+5s-5s^2.\]

At ground level, \(5s^2-5s-18=0\). The positive root is \(s=(5+\sqrt{385})/10\), and horizontal motion has constant leftward speed 2. Thus the distance travelled is \(2s=(5+\sqrt{385})/5\) m.

For another meeting with the infinite line containing the barrier, set \(y=x-18\). This gives \(7s-5s^2=0\), whose later root is \(s=7/5\). At that time \(x=166/5=33.2\lt 34\), outside the finite segment. The ball therefore does not hit the barrier a second time.
questions.hint_html: For an inclined smooth barrier, resolve parallel and perpendicular to the barrier before applying restitution. Afterwards start a new flight clock at the impact.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the signed vertical velocity to obtain the time.
Find the vertical coordinate and identify the impact point.
Combine the two components using the speed formula.
Obtain the two incoming components parallel and normal to the barrier.
Resolve the new components into horizontal and vertical directions.
Solve the new vertical-motion equation for the positive landing time.
Use the magnitude of the horizontal velocity to find the distance.
Check that the later line intersection lies outside the actual segment.

questions.title: Which positions of a short wall cause an impact?
questions.prompt_html:
Throughout free flight, neglect air resistance and take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), vertically downwards.

A particle is projected from level ground at angle \(\theta\), where \(\tan\theta=3/2\). It passes through the point \((12,12)\), measured in metres from its launch point using horizontal and upward vertical axes. Later in the same flight it strikes the vertical face of a wall of height 6 m at horizontal coordinate \(x=D\). Contact with the top of the wall is allowed, but contact at ground level is not counted as striking its face.

  1. Find the initial speed squared, \(u^2\), and the equation of the trajectory.

    [2]

  2. Find the complete set of possible values of \(D\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(u^2=390\), and \(y=\frac32x-\frac{x^2}{24}\).

(b)

\(18+6\sqrt5\le D\lt 36\), in metres.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Use \(\sec^2\theta=1+(3/2)^2=13/4\). The trajectory equation is

\[y=\frac32x-\frac{65x^2}{4u^2}.\]

At \((12,12)\), \(12=18-2340/u^2\), so \(u^2=390\). Substitution then gives \(y=3x/2-x^2/24\).

Part (b)

Striking the wall face requires \(0\lt y(D)\le6\). Also, the wall is met after the point at \(x=12\), so \(D\gt 12\).

The upper-height condition is

\[\frac32D-\frac{D^2}{24}\le6\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad D^2-36D+144\ge0.\]

The roots are \(18\pm6\sqrt5\). Since the quadratic opens upwards, its nonnegative ranges lie outside the two roots. The smaller branch is incompatible with \(D\gt 12\).

The particle returns to ground at \(x=36\), so the strict condition \(y(D)\gt 0\) excludes \(D=36\). The top-contact boundary is included. Therefore

\[18+6\sqrt5\le D\lt 36.\]
questions.hint_html: It is not enough to solve \(y=6\). Also use “later”, positive height, and the definition of contact at the top.

marking_criteria.description_html: Substitute the point into the trajectory equation.
Find the speed squared and simplify the trajectory.
Translate contact into the correct height inequalities.
Use the order of events to reject the early branch.

questions.title: Clearing a wall with the shortest landing range
questions.prompt_html:
Throughout free flight, neglect air resistance and take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), vertically downwards.

A particle is projected from level ground with speed \(20\sqrt2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at an acute angle \(\theta\). A vertical wall 20 m high stands 40 m from the launch point. For this question “clears the wall” includes passing exactly through its top; the particle is treated as a point.

  1. Find the two angles for which the particle passes exactly through the top of the wall.

    [3]

  2. Find the least horizontal range among the trajectories that clear the wall, justifying which angle gives it.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\theta=45^\circ\) or \(\theta=\tan^{-1}3\approx71.6^\circ\).

(b)

The least range is \(48\) m, attained when \(\tan\theta=3\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Let \(z=\tan\theta\gt 0\). At the wall, the trajectory gives

\[20=40z-10(1+z^2).\]

Hence \(z^2-4z+3=0\), so \(z=1\) or \(z=3\). The corresponding acute angles are \(45^\circ\) and \(\tan^{-1}3\).

Part (b)

Clearing the wall requires \(40z-10(1+z^2)\ge20\), so \(1\le z\le3\). The range is

\[R=\frac{u^2}{g}\sin2\theta=\frac{160z}{1+z^2}.\]

Its derivative is \(160(1-z^2)/(1+z^2)^2\), which is nonpositive on \([1,3]\) and negative for \(z\gt 1\). Therefore the minimum is at \(z=3\): \(R=480/10=48\) m.

Including top contact makes this minimum attainable. If strictly positive clearance were required, 48 m would instead be an infimum.
questions.hint_html: The two top-grazing trajectories delimit the admissible angles. Do not assume that the smaller launch angle gives the shorter range.

marking_criteria.description_html: Substitute the wall coordinates into the trajectory equation.
Obtain the permitted interval of angles or tangent values.
Justify how the range varies over that interval.

questions.title: Two angles, different directions at the same target
questions.prompt_html:
Throughout free flight, neglect air resistance and take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), vertically downwards.

A particle is projected from \(O\) with speed \(u\) at an acute angle \(\alpha\). Use horizontal and upward vertical coordinates through \(O\).

  1. Derive the Cartesian equation of its trajectory by eliminating time.

    [3]

  2. For \(u=5\sqrt{30}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), find the possible values of \(\tan\alpha\) if the particle passes through \((30,18)\).

    [3]

  3. For each value, state whether the particle is rising or falling as it passes through the target.

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(y=x\tan\alpha-\dfrac{gx^2}{2u^2}(1+\tan^2\alpha)\).

(b)

\(\tan\alpha=1\) or \(\tan\alpha=4\).

(c)

Rising when \(\tan\alpha=1\); falling when \(\tan\alpha=4\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Horizontal and vertical motion give \(x=u\cos\alpha\,t\) and \(y=u\sin\alpha\,t-gt^2/2\). Since \(\cos\alpha\gt 0\), eliminate \(t=x/(u\cos\alpha)\):

\[y=x\tan\alpha-\frac{gx^2}{2u^2\cos^2\alpha}.\]

Using \(1/\cos^2\alpha=1+\tan^2\alpha\) gives the stated form.

Part (b)

Here \(u^2=750\), \(g=10\), and \((x,y)=(30,18)\). With \(z=\tan\alpha\),

\[18=30z-6(1+z^2).\]

Thus \(z^2-5z+4=0\), giving \(z=1\) or \(z=4\). Both are positive and correspond to acute launch angles.

Part (c)

At \(x=30\), the trajectory gradient is \(z-(2/5)(1+z^2)\). It equals \(1/5\gt 0\) when \(z=1\), and \(-14/5\lt 0\) when \(z=4\). Since horizontal velocity is positive, these signs mean rising and falling respectively.
questions.hint_html: Treat the trajectory as a quadratic in \(\tan\alpha\). The sign of its gradient at the target identifies the branch of flight.

marking_criteria.description_html: Express the result in terms of the tangent.
Form the quadratic from the target data.
Correctly classify both crossings using the sign of the gradient or vertical velocity.

questions.title: Recovering speed from two heights
questions.prompt_html:
Throughout free flight, neglect air resistance and take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), vertically downwards.

A particle is launched from level ground at angle \(\theta\), where \(\tan\theta=3/2\), with unknown speed \(u\). At horizontal distance 20 m its height is \(H\) metres. At horizontal distance 50 m its height is \(5H/8\). Both observations occur before the first return to ground.

  1. Find \(u\) and \(H\).

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(u=5\sqrt{26}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), \(H=20\) m.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Write the trajectory as \(y=3x/2-cx^2\), where

\[c=\frac{g(1+\tan^2\theta)}{2u^2}=\frac{65}{4u^2}\gt 0.\]

The two height readings give

\[H=30-400c,\qquad \frac58H=75-2500c.\]

Substitute the first into the second:

\[\frac58(30-400c)=75-2500c.\]

Thus \(2250c=225/4\), so \(c=1/40\). Hence \(H=30-10=20\) and \(65/(4u^2)=1/40\), giving \(u^2=650\), or \(u=5\sqrt{26}\).

The resulting trajectory returns to ground at \(x=60\), so both observations occur during the flight.
questions.hint_html: Introduce one constant for the coefficient of \(x^2\). Eliminate \(H\) before solving for the launch speed.

Eliminate the unknown height and find the quadratic coefficient.

questions.title: A second launch after one third of the flight
questions.prompt_html:
Throughout free flight, neglect air resistance and take the acceleration due to gravity to be \(g\), vertically downwards.

Particle \(P\) is projected from \(O\) on level ground with speed \(u\) at angle \(\theta\), where \(\tan\theta=1/2\). It passes through the point \((4a,3a/2)\), where \(a\gt 0\) is a length. After \(P\) has completed one third of its total flight time, a second particle \(Q\) is launched from \(O\) in the same vertical plane. Both particles land at the same point at the same instant. Write \(V\) and \(\alpha\) for the speed and acute angle of projection of \(Q\).

  1. Use the given point to find \(u^2\) in terms of \(a\) and \(g\).

    [3]

  2. Find \(V^2\) and \(\tan\alpha\).

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(u^2=20ag\).

(b)

\(V^2=340ag/9\), \(\tan\alpha=2/9\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The trajectory of \(P\) is

\[y=\frac{x}{2}-\frac{5gx^2}{8u^2}.\]

At \((4a,3a/2)\), this gives \(3a/2=2a-10ga^2/u^2\). Hence \(u^2=20ag\).

Part (b)

Let the initial components of \(P\) be \(p_x=2u/\sqrt5\) and \(p_y=u/\sqrt5\). Its total flight time is \(F=2p_y/g\), and its range is \(R=p_xF\).

Particle \(Q\) has only \(2F/3\) seconds available. To cover the same horizontal distance, it must have horizontal component

\[q_x=\frac{R}{2F/3}=\frac32p_x.\]

Since \(Q\) starts and finishes at ground level, its vertical component must satisfy \(2q_y/g=2F/3\), giving \(q_y=2p_y/3\).

Therefore

\[V^2=q_x^2+q_y^2=\frac94\frac{4u^2}{5}+\frac49\frac{u^2}{5}=\frac{17u^2}{9}=\frac{340ag}{9}.\]

Also \(\tan\alpha=q_y/q_x=(4/9)(p_y/p_x)=2/9\). The delayed launch changes the two components by different factors, so its angle is not the same as that of \(P\).
questions.hint_html: Equal landing times do not mean equal flight durations. Determine the two components of the later projectile separately.

marking_criteria.description_html: Form the trajectory using the known angle.
Combine components and substitute for the original speed squared.

questions.title: Launching from beneath the first apex
questions.prompt_html:
Throughout free flight, neglect air resistance and take the acceleration due to gravity to be \(g\), vertically downwards.

Particle \(P\) is projected from \(O\) on horizontal ground with speed \(u\), where \(\tan\theta=3/2\) for its launch angle. It passes through \((4a,11a/2)\), where \(a\gt 0\). Its horizontal range is \(R\).

At the instant when \(P\) is at its highest point, particle \(Q\) is launched to the right from the point \(B=(R/2,0)\), vertically below that highest point. The two particles reach the ground together at \((R,0)\). Let \(V\) and \(\alpha\) be the speed and angle of projection of \(Q\).

  1. Find \(u^2\).

    [3]

  2. Find \(R\) in terms of \(a\).

    [2]

  3. Find \(V\) and \(\tan\alpha\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(u^2=52ag\).

(b)

\(R=48a\).

(c)

\(V=5\sqrt{ag}\), \(\tan\alpha=3/4\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Using \(\tan\theta=3/2\), the trajectory is \(y=3x/2-13gx^2/(8u^2)\). Substitution of the given point gives

\[\frac{11a}{2}=6a-\frac{26ga^2}{u^2}.\]

Thus \(26ga^2/u^2=a/2\), and \(u^2=52ag\).

Part (b)

The initial components of \(P\) are \(2u/\sqrt{13}\) and \(3u/\sqrt{13}\). Consequently

\[R=\frac{2}{g}\frac{2u}{\sqrt{13}}\frac{3u}{\sqrt{13}}=\frac{12u^2}{13g}=48a.\]

Part (c)

Write \(p_x=2u/\sqrt{13}\) and \(p_y=3u/\sqrt{13}\). The remaining time from the apex is \(p_y/g\). Particle \(Q\) must cover only half the range, \(R/2=p_xp_y/g\), so its horizontal component is \(q_x=p_x\).

Its flight starts and ends on the ground. Therefore \(2q_y/g=p_y/g\), giving \(q_y=p_y/2\). Thus

\[V^2=p_x^2+\frac14p_y^2=\frac{4u^2}{13}+\frac{9u^2}{52}=\frac{25u^2}{52}=25ag.\]

Taking the positive root gives \(V=5\sqrt{ag}\), and \(\tan\alpha=(p_y/2)/p_x=3/4\).
questions.hint_html: The second particle starts below the first apex, not at \(O\). It has half the range and half the original flight time to complete.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the trajectory with the correct angle factor.
Use the correct remaining time and horizontal distance.

questions.title: Two launch settings and an unknown obstacle
questions.prompt_html:
Throughout free flight, neglect air resistance and take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), vertically downwards.

A launcher fires particles from level ground at the same unknown acute angle \(\theta\), using two different speeds. At a point 16 m horizontally from the launcher, the shot with speed \(20\sqrt2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) is at height \(h\), exactly the obstacle height. The shot with speed \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) is at height \(2h/3\) at that same horizontal position.

  1. With \(z=\tan\theta\), obtain two equations involving \(h\) and \(z\).

    [3]

  2. Find the two possible obstacle heights and the corresponding values of \(\tan\theta\).

    [4]

  3. For each possible setting, find the greatest height of the faster shot.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(h=16z-\frac85(1+z^2)\), \(2h/3=16z-\frac{16}{5}(1+z^2)\).

(b)

\((h,\tan\theta)=(6,1/2)\) or \((24,2)\), with heights in metres.

(c)

\(8\) m for \(\tan\theta=1/2\), and \(32\) m for \(\tan\theta=2\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Eliminating time from \(x=u\cos\theta\,t\) and \(y=u\sin\theta\,t-5t^2\) gives \(y=xz-5x^2(1+z^2)/u^2\).

At \(x=16\), the two values of \(u^2\) are 800 and 400. Thus

\[h=16z-\frac85(1+z^2),\]
\[\frac23h=16z-\frac{16}{5}(1+z^2).\]

Part (b)

Twice the first equation minus the second eliminates \(1+z^2\): \(4h/3=16z\), so \(h=12z\).

Substitution into the first equation gives

\[12z=16z-\frac85(1+z^2),\]

or \(2z^2-5z+2=0\). Thus \(z=1/2\) or \(z=2\). Both angles are acute and both heights positive. Using \(h=12z\), the corresponding heights are 6 m and 24 m.

Part (c)

For the faster shot, \(u^2=800\). Therefore

\[H=\frac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}=40\frac{z^2}{1+z^2}.\]

At \(z=1/2\), \(H=8\) m. At \(z=2\), \(H=32\) m. In each case the obstacle height is three quarters of that shot's maximum height.
questions.hint_html: The angle is the same for the two shots. Form the two height equations and eliminate their common quadratic expression.

marking_criteria.description_html: Eliminate one expression to obtain a relation between height and tangent.
Express maximum height in terms of the tangent.

questions.title: A second angle at the same launch speed
questions.prompt_html:
Throughout free flight, neglect air resistance and take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), vertically downwards.

A particle projected from level ground must pass through \(A=(24,12)\) m. At one possible launch angle, \(\tan\theta=2\). The launch speed is to be kept fixed while the angle is changed.

  1. Derive the trajectory equation in the form \(y=xz-\frac{gx^2}{2u^2}(1+z^2)\), where \(z=\tan\theta\).

    [3]

  2. Find the launch speed and the other possible value of \(\tan\theta\).

    [4]

  3. Which launch angle reaches \(A\) first? Give the two flight times to \(A\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(y=xz-\dfrac{gx^2}{2u^2}(1+z^2)\).

(b)

\(u=20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and the other value is \(4/3\).

(c)

The angle with \(\tan\theta=4/3\) arrives first: \(2\) s, compared with \(6\sqrt5/5\) s for \(\tan\theta=2\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The displacement equations are \(x=u\cos\theta\,t\) and \(y=u\sin\theta\,t-gt^2/2\). Substitute \(t=x/(u\cos\theta)\) into the second equation to obtain

\[y=x\tan\theta-\frac{gx^2}{2u^2}\sec^2\theta.\]

Finally use \(\sec^2\theta=1+\tan^2\theta\) and \(z=\tan\theta\).

Part (b)

For the given value \(z=2\), substituting \(A\) gives

\[12=48-\frac{10(24)^2}{2u^2}(5),\]

so \(u^2=400\) and \(u=20\). Keeping this speed fixed, the target equation becomes

\[12=24z-\frac{36}{5}(1+z^2).\]

Hence \(3z^2-10z+8=(3z-4)(z-2)=0\). The other value is \(z=4/3\). Both roots correspond to acute angles and positive target heights before landing.

Part (c)

For \(\tan\theta=2\), the horizontal component is \(20/\sqrt5\), so the time to \(x=24\) is \(6\sqrt5/5\) s.

For \(\tan\theta=4/3\), the horizontal component is \(20(3/5)=12\), so the time is 2 s. Since \(6\sqrt5/5\gt 2\), the smaller angle reaches the target first.
questions.hint_html: First use the known angle to determine the fixed speed. Only then solve a new quadratic for the unknown angle.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the supplied angle to determine the speed squared.
Obtain the new quadratic for the fixed speed.
Obtain both target times from horizontal motion.
Compare them and identify the earlier trajectory.

questions.title: A range-to-height ratio and shallow directions
questions.prompt_html:
Throughout free flight, neglect air resistance and take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), vertically downwards.

A particle is projected from level ground with speed \(u\) at acute angle \(\theta\). Let \(R\) be its horizontal range and \(H\) its greatest height. It is known that \(R=3H\).

  1. Obtain expressions for \(R\) and \(H\), and hence relate \(R/H\) to \(\theta\).

    [3]

  2. Find \(\tan\theta\).

    [2]

  3. Now \(u=25\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the set of horizontal positions \(x\) during the flight for which the smaller, non-negative angle between the direction of motion and the horizontal is less than \(\tan^{-1}(1/2)\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(R=2u^2\sin\theta\cos\theta/g\), \(H=u^2\sin^2\theta/(2g)\), so \(R/H=4\cot\theta\).

(b)

\(\tan\theta=4/3\).

(c)

\(75/4\lt x\lt 165/4\), in metres.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The nonzero root of \(0=u\sin\theta\,t-gt^2/2\) is \(t_f=2u\sin\theta/g\). Hence the horizontal range is \(R=u\cos\theta\,t_f=2u^2\sin\theta\cos\theta/g\).

At the top, zero vertical velocity gives \(2gH=u^2\sin^2\theta\). Dividing the expressions yields \(R/H=4\cot\theta\).

Part (b)

Using \(R/H=3\), the preceding relation gives \(4\cot\theta=3\). Since the angle is acute, \(\tan\theta=4/3\), with \(\sin\theta=4/5\) and \(\cos\theta=3/5\).

Part (c)

The initial components are 15 and 20. At horizontal position \(x\), \(t=x/15\), so the gradient of the direction of motion is

\[\frac{v_y}{v_x}=\frac{20-10x/15}{15}=\frac43-\frac{2x}{45}.\]

The condition concerns the acute angle on either side of the top, so the magnitude of this gradient must be less than \(1/2\):

\[-\frac12\lt \frac43-\frac{2x}{45}\lt \frac12.\]

Solving both inequalities gives \(75/4\lt x\lt 165/4\). The entire flight lies in \(0\le x\le60\), so no further truncation is needed. Both endpoints are excluded because the requested angle inequality is strict.
questions.hint_html: The direction can be above or below horizontal. Convert the angle condition into a bound on the absolute value of the gradient.

marking_criteria.description_html: Obtain the direction gradient in terms of horizontal position.
Use its absolute value and a strict two-sided inequality.

questions.title: A string is cut before the highest point
questions.prompt_html:
Throughout free flight, neglect air resistance and take the acceleration due to gravity to be \(g\), vertically downwards.

A particle of mass \(m\) is attached to a fixed point \(O\) by a light inextensible string of length \(a\). It starts at \(B=(0,-a)\), directly below \(O\), and is projected horizontally to the right. As it rises round the right-hand part of the circle, the string is cut at \(D=(4a/5,3a/5)\). Just after the cut its velocity is tangential, directed leftwards and upwards, and has magnitude \(V\). In the subsequent free flight it passes through \(A=(0,a)\).

  1. Find \(V^2\) in terms of \(a\) and \(g\).

    [4]

  2. Find the tension immediately after launch at \(B\), and check that the string can remain taut until it is cut.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(V^2=4ag/3\).

(b)

Initial tension \(=83mg/15\); tension just before the cut \(=11mg/15\gt 0\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The radius to \(D\) has horizontal and vertical ratios \(4/5\) and \(3/5\). A perpendicular tangent directed left and up therefore gives velocity components \(-3V/5\) and \(4V/5\).

To travel from \(x=4a/5\) to \(x=0\), the required time is \(t=4a/(3V)\). The required vertical rise is \(a-3a/5=2a/5\), so

\[\frac{2a}{5}=\frac{4V}{5}\frac{4a}{3V}-\frac12g\left(\frac{4a}{3V}\right)^2.\]

Thus \(2a/5=16a/15-8ga^2/(9V^2)\), giving \(V^2=4ag/3\).

Part (b)

Let the initial speed at \(B\) be \(w\). The rise from \(B\) to \(D\) is \(8a/5\). Conservation of energy before the cut gives

\[w^2=V^2+\frac{16ag}{5}=\frac{68ag}{15}.\]

At the bottom the inward direction is upwards, so \(T_B-mg=mw^2/a\). Therefore \(T_B=mg+mw^2/a=83mg/15\).

At \(D\), weight has inward component \(3mg/5\). Hence \(T_D+3mg/5=mV^2/a\), giving \(T_D=11mg/15\gt 0\).

Along the rising arc the tension decreases as the height increases: using energy, at height \(y\) relative to \(O\), \(T=mw^2/a-2mg-3mgy/a\). Its least value before the cut is therefore \(T_D\gt 0\). The string stays taut. It is cut deliberately, not released by zero tension.
questions.hint_html: After the cut, use the tangent as the initial projectile direction. Before the cut, use energy and the inward radial force equation.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use horizontal displacement to find the time.
Use the correct rise in the energy equation.
Find the bottom tension from the radial equation.
Calculate the positive tension immediately before the cut.
Justify that tension is no smaller earlier on the rising arc.

questions.title: Reaching another trajectory’s highest point
questions.prompt_html:
Throughout free flight, neglect air resistance and take the acceleration due to gravity to be \(g\), vertically downwards.

A launcher fires particles from \(O\) on horizontal ground with a fixed speed \(u\). The angle of projection may be changed. Let \(Q\) be the highest point of the trajectory obtained when the launch angle \(\theta\) satisfies \(\tan\theta=1/2\).

  1. Derive the trajectory equation for a general acute launch angle \(\alpha\).

    [3]

  2. Find the coordinates of \(Q\).

    [3]

  3. Find the other acute launch angle for which the particle passes through \(Q\). State whether it is rising or falling at \(Q\) for this other angle.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(y=x\tan\alpha-\dfrac{gx^2}{2u^2}(1+\tan^2\alpha)\).

(b)

\(Q=(2u^2/(5g),\ u^2/(10g))\).

(c)

The other angle is \(\tan^{-1}(9/2)\). The particle is falling at \(Q\), where its direction gradient is \(-4\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The displacement equations are \(x=u\cos\alpha\,t\) and \(y=u\sin\alpha\,t-gt^2/2\). Eliminating \(t\) gives

\[y=x\tan\alpha-\frac{gx^2}{2u^2}\sec^2\alpha=x\tan\alpha-\frac{gx^2}{2u^2}(1+\tan^2\alpha).\]

Part (b)

For the specified trajectory, \(\sin\theta=1/\sqrt5\) and \(\cos\theta=2/\sqrt5\). The apex time is \(u/(g\sqrt5)\). Therefore

\[x_Q=\frac{2u}{\sqrt5}\frac{u}{g\sqrt5}=\frac{2u^2}{5g},\qquad y_Q=\frac{(u/\sqrt5)^2}{2g}=\frac{u^2}{10g}.\]

Part (c)

Put \(z=\tan\alpha\) and substitute the coordinates of \(Q\) into the general trajectory. Cancelling \(u^2/g\) gives

\[\frac1{10}=\frac25z-\frac2{25}(1+z^2).\]

Thus \(4z^2-20z+9=(2z-1)(2z-9)=0\). One root is the original \(z=1/2\); the other is \(z=9/2\).

The trajectory gradient at \(Q\) is

\[z-\frac{gx_Q}{u^2}(1+z^2)=\frac92-\frac25\left(1+\frac{81}{4}\right)=-4.\]

Horizontal velocity is positive, so this negative gradient means that the particle is falling.
questions.hint_html: The point \(Q\) stays fixed when the angle is changed. It need not be the highest point of the new trajectory.

marking_criteria.description_html: Find the apex time or use the apex condition.
Substitute the same target into the fixed-speed trajectory.
Form and solve the quadratic in the tangent.
Use the signed velocity or gradient to classify the crossing.

questions.title: An inaccessible target at the same speed
questions.prompt_html:
Throughout free flight, neglect air resistance and take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), vertically downwards.

A particle is launched from level ground with speed \(u\) at angle \(\theta\) where \(\tan\theta=3\). It passes through \(A=(12,24)\) m. A second shot is made with the same speed but an arbitrary acute angle \(\alpha\).

  1. Find \(u^2\).

    [3]

  2. Show that the second shot cannot pass through \(B=(30,30)\) m, whatever acute angle is chosen. Do not assume a formula for an envelope of trajectories.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(u^2=600\).

(b)

The required equation is \(z^2-4z+5=0\), where \(z=\tan\alpha\). Its discriminant is \(-4\), so there is no real launch angle.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

For the first angle, \(\sec^2\theta=10\), so its trajectory is

\[y=3x-\frac{50x^2}{u^2}.\]

At \(A\), \(24=36-7200/u^2\). Hence \(u^2=600\).

Part (b)

With \(z=\tan\alpha\) and \(u^2=600\), passing through \(B\) would require

\[30=30z-\frac{15}{2}(1+z^2).\]

This simplifies to \(z^2-4z+5=0\). Its discriminant is \(16-20=-4\lt 0\). Thus no real value of \(z\), and in particular no positive value corresponding to an acute angle, is possible.

Alternatively, at this particular horizontal position,

\[y=30z-\frac{15}{2}(1+z^2)=\frac{45}{2}-\frac{15}{2}(z-2)^2\le\frac{45}{2}\lt 30.\]

This is a calculation for the specified target coordinate only; no general bounding-parabola formula is used.
questions.hint_html: Keep the speed fixed, but replace the angle by a new variable. The target equation must have a real positive tangent solution.

Substitute the new target using the unchanged speed.
Obtain the quadratic in the new tangent.
Evaluate its discriminant or complete the square.
Conclude that no admissible projection angle exists.
